about: Trainer: particle-level equilibrium and kinetics (Units 5 and 7). Explore: a sealed vessel of moving particles for a real gas-phase reaction; temperature, volume, amounts and a catalyst change the rates (Arrhenius) and K (van 't Hoff); Q moves to K on a live graph. Test yourself: seeded predict-then-run problems from ApChemMath.eqk.generate, rechecked by scripts/lib/apchem-tool-checks/equilibrium-kinetics.mjs.

sources.n2o4: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g): ΔH° = +57.2 kJ/mol and ΔG° = +4.73 kJ/mol at 298.15 K from the standard enthalpies and Gibbs energies of formation (NO2 33.18 and 51.31, N2O4 9.16 and 97.89 kJ/mol; NBS Tables of Chemical Thermodynamic Properties, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 11, suppl. 2, 1982, as in the CRC Handbook), so Kp = 0.146 at 298.15 K (atm). Forward activation energy taken as 65 kJ/mol, a little above ΔH°, because the recombination of two NO2 has only a small barrier (7.8 kJ/mol here; measured recombination barriers are near zero, so this is rounded up to leave room for the catalyst). The catalyst's 6 kJ/mol drop is illustrative.
sources.hi: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g): Kc = 54.3 at 430 °C (703 K), the classic value (Taylor and Crist, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 63, 1377, 1941, give 54.4 at 698.6 K); ΔH° = −9.5 kJ/mol from the enthalpies of formation of HI(g) (26.48) and I2(g) (62.44 kJ/mol), NBS 1982. Activation energy of 2 HI → H2 + I2 about 184 kJ/mol (Kistiakowsky; Bodenstein), so about 175 kJ/mol forward. The catalyst's 12 kJ/mol drop is illustrative (a metal surface lowers it far more).
sources.model: K at other temperatures: van 't Hoff with ΔH° held constant (ln K2/K1 = −ΔH°/R (1/T2 − 1/T1)), on Kp, then Kc = Kp/(RT)^Δn. Rates: rate forward = kf × [reactants] to their coefficients, rate reverse = kr × [products] to theirs, with kf = A e^(−Ea/RT) and kr = kf/Kc, so the net rate is zero exactly when Q = K. The catalyst is illustrative, and never more than the reverse barrier: it lowers Ea for both directions by the same amount (so K is unchanged). Time is scaled so a run takes seconds; the RATIOS between temperatures and with the catalyst are the real Arrhenius ratios.
sources.mb: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular kinetic energies in a gas: f(E) = 2 (E/π)^½ (RT)^(−3/2) e^(−E/RT); the share at or above Ea is erfc(√x) + 2√(x/π) e^(−x), x = Ea/RT.

intro: Watch an equilibrium at the particle level. Molecules move faster when it is hotter, collide, and only collisions with enough energy react. Change the temperature, the volume or the amounts, or add a catalyst, and see Q move away from K and the mixture shift until Q = K again.
howItWorks:
Q < K: net forward. Q > K: net reverse. Q = K: equilibrium (both reactions still run, at equal rates).

  • Amounts and volume change Q, not K. Compressing a gas mixture raises Q when there are more gas particles on the product side, so the mixture shifts toward fewer gas particles.
  • Temperature changes K. For an endothermic reaction K rises with temperature; for an exothermic one it falls. Temperature also changes how fast both directions run.
  • A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions by the same amount: equilibrium is reached sooner, at the same position. K and Q do not change.
  • The energy graph shows the share of molecules with at least Ea. Heating moves the curve right, so that share grows quickly.

Real data: see the sources in the tool's data file. Time is scaled so each run takes seconds, but the speed-ups from heating and from the catalyst are the real Arrhenius ratios.

tint.what: NO₂ is a brown gas; N₂O₄ is colorless
I₂ vapor is violet; H₂ and HI are colorless
